John à Lasco
JON ah LAS-koh
n. proper (Polish Reformed Reformer; 1499–1560)
Johannes à Lasco is the Latinized form of Jan Łaski (Polish), from the place-name Łask in central Poland; the name Jan is the Polish form of John (Hebrew Yōḥanān, “the LORD is gracious”). The Latinization a Lasco signals his Polish noble origin and his use of the humanist scholarly convention of place-surnames.

Biblical Definition

John à Lasco (Jan Łaski, 1499–1560) was a Polish nobleman, humanist, and Reformed churchman who became one of the most cosmopolitan figures of the sixteenth-century Reformation. Nephew of the powerful Archbishop Jan Łaski of Gniezno, John renounced his expected Catholic career after extensive contact with Erasmus and, decisively, with Heinrich Bullinger and Martin Bucer. He served as Superintendent of Reformed churches in East Friesland (1542–1549), building one of the most fully developed Reformed church orders on the continent — an order grounded in church discipline, catechesis, and congregational participation. When Edward VI opened England to the Reformation, à Lasco was invited to superintend the “stranger churches” in London (1550–1553), communities of French and Dutch Protestant exiles. His Forma ac Ratio (published 1555) is among the most detailed accounts of a functioning Reformed polity from the period, including elder governance, discipline, and Lord's Supper practice. Mary I's accession drove him back to the continent; he labored briefly in Denmark and the Baltic before returning to Poland in 1556, where he led the Reformed minority church until his death. His life embodied the ecumenical Reformed vision of the mid-sixteenth century — not Lutheranism and not Rome but a catholic Protestantism governed by Scripture, anchored in the ancient creeds, administered through elder-governance and church discipline.

Webster 1828 Definition

Polish nobleman and Reformed churchman who superintended the stranger churches in Edwardian London and left behind in the Forma ac Ratio one of the most detailed accounts of functioning Reformed polity in the sixteenth century; his career illustrated the transnational, elder-governed, discipline-centered vision of the continental and English Reformation.

LASCO, John à (1499–1560). Jan Łaski; Polish Reformed Reformer, Superintendent of the East Friesland churches and of the London stranger churches under Edward VI. Born into the Polish nobility, he was expected to follow his uncle, Archbishop Jan Łaski, into a Catholic ecclesiastical career; contact with Erasmus in Basel and with Bullinger and Bucer on the continent diverted him into Reformation territory.

His East Friesland superintendency (1542–1549) produced one of the most complete Reformed church orders of the era: he insisted on lay elder involvement in governance, regular church discipline (not merely doctrinal subscription), and catechesis as the foundation of church life. These features — not novel but unusually well-organized — made East Friesland a model.

In England (1550–1553), Cranmer's invitation gave him oversight of the French and Dutch stranger churches in London. The Forma ac Ratio (written during this period, published Emden 1555) is a primary source for what elder-governed, discipline-practicing, catechism-centered Reformed worship actually looked like in the mid-sixteenth century.

Mary's persecution drove him north to Denmark, then to Frankfurt and Emden, then finally home to Poland (1556), where he organized the Reformed minority under fierce Catholic pressure. His transnational career embodied the Reformed vision of one Reformation across national boundaries, united by doctrine and discipline rather than by territorial confession.

Among Reformation figures of the second rank, à Lasco stands as evidence that the Reformed churches were never merely national or parochial; they were a genuinely catholic (universal) communion ordered by Scripture, which is why a Polish nobleman could superintend French and Dutch exiles in London and still be entirely at home.

Matthew 18:17 — "And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican."

Acts 6:3 — "Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business."

Titus 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Acts 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Modern Corruption

Ecumenical histories flatten à Lasco into a generic “irenic humanist” figure, obscuring the confessional sharpness of his Reformed ecclesiology and his insistence on church discipline as non-negotiable — a feature modern broad-church Protestantism is eager to soft-pedal.

expand to see more

Because à Lasco maintained courteous relations with Lutherans while disagreeing with them on the Lord's Supper, ecumenical historians have sometimes pressed him into service as an early ecumenist avant la lettre — a man who saw beyond confessional boundaries. This misreads both the man and the era. His irenic tone was the courtesy of a nobleman who believed truth mattered too much for needless combat; it was not theological latitudinarianism. He held the Reformed position on the Lord's Supper with clarity and defended it publicly. Courtesy and conviction coexisted in him as they should in every Reformed minister.

More damaging is the modern ecumenical tendency to praise à Lasco's “inclusive” approach to the stranger churches while ignoring that those churches practiced formal church discipline — the mechanism that made fellowship meaningful rather than merely nominal. His Forma ac Ratio gives extensive space to the procedure for admonition and excommunication. An à Lasco stripped of church discipline is a caricature manufactured for a therapeutic ecclesiology that cannot bear the thought that love sometimes says no.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Educated in Polish nobility and Basel humanism, formed in Reformed doctrine by Bullinger and Bucer, à Lasco's church orders drew on continental Reformed ecclesiology and became primary sources for English-speaking and Polish Reformed church life.

expand to see more

Polish nobility — born into the Łaski family, one of Poland's most powerful noble houses; his uncle Archbishop Jan Łaski wielded enormous ecclesiastical power; the young Jan was destined for a similar career until Reformation theology captured him.

Erasmus and Basel humanism — à Lasco spent time with Erasmus at Basel (c.1524), inheriting humanist textual methods and a passion for reform from within, though he moved well beyond Erasmus's hesitant reform by embracing the Reformation's doctrinal substance.

Bullinger and Bucer — his decisive Reformed formation came through sustained contact with Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich and Martin Bucer of Strasbourg; from them he took the Reformed insistence on church discipline, elder governance, and a memorial-with-presence Lord's Supper theology.

Forma ac Ratio (1555) — his primary published legacy; a detailed liturgical and polity order for the London stranger churches, covering the Lord's Supper, baptism, catechesis, church discipline, and elder election; a major primary source for sixteenth-century Reformed worship.

Poland and the Reformed minority — his final years (1556–1560) organizing the Polish Reformed church under Catholic pressure gave continental Protestantism its most visible example of a confessional Reformed minority operating without state support, governed by Scripture and discipline alone.

Usage

"The stranger churches under à Lasco demonstrate that Reformed polity is not a product of political establishment but of theological conviction — his congregations were refugees without political power, yet they maintained elder governance, catechesis, and church discipline."

"The Forma ac Ratio remains a primary source for historians of Reformed worship and polity, documenting what the Reformation looked like on the ground — not in theological treatises alone but in the actual ordering of weekly gathered worship."

"His career reminds Reformed believers that the Reformation was a genuinely ecumenical (catholic) movement: the same doctrines and the same polity could unite a Polish nobleman, French Huguenots, Dutch refugees, and English Puritans under the Word of God."
